questions.question: What are the most important exception handling best practices in Java?
questions.title: Java Exception Handling Best Practices
questions.direct_answer: Catch an exception only where you can recover, translate it, add useful context, or handle it at a boundary. Do not swallow it. Preserve the cause when wrapping, use specific types, clean up with try-with-resources, and usually log once at the boundary that finally handles the failure—not in every layer that rethrows it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Code quality awareness — does the candidate write production-quality exception handling that helps debugging
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking exception handling is just adding try-catch wherever the compiler complains, without considering maintainability
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give specific anti-patterns with code examples and explain why each practice matters in production

sections.title: What Exception Best Practices Actually Are
sections.content:
Good exception handling keeps the original failure understandable and handles it at the right layer. Catch an exception only when the current code can recover, translate it into a more meaningful abstraction, add context that is not already available, or turn it into an external response at a boundary. Otherwise let it propagate.

Do not use an empty catch block. When translating, pass the original exception as the cause. Prefer specific exception types so callers can distinguish failures. Use try-with-resources for closeable resources.

Logging is not required in every catch block. If a lower layer logs and rethrows, an upper layer often logs the same failure again. Usually the boundary that finally handles the failure—such as a job runner or HTTP exception handler—logs it once with the exception object and relevant request context.

sections.title: What to Do With a Caught Exception
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A[Exception caught] --> B{Can you handle it here?} B -- No --> C[Rethrow and wrap
new ServiceException msg, cause] B -- Yes --> D[Log once with the exception object] C --> E[Boundary handler logs it once] D --> F[Return a clear error response] E --> F style A fill:#fde68a style F fill:#bbf7d0 ```

sections.title: Java Exception Handling Best Practices at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Never swallow|~empty catch is evil|log when this layer owns the final handling decision or rethrow|silent failure -> bad state|the hardest bug to find
blue|Be specific|~catch what you handle|not Exception or Throwable|Throwable catches OOM|let the unexpected propagate
emerald|Preserve cause|~chain the trace|new X(msg, cause)|not new X(e.getMessage())|keeps the root cause
rose|Log once|~at the boundary|controller / global handler|not in every layer|descriptive messages

sections.title: Wrong: swallowing the error and losing the cause
Right: specific catch, log with context, wrap with the cause
When to Apply These Practices
sections.content:
Apply these practices in **service layer methods** where business logic executes — this is where most application errors occur and need clear handling.

Use **specific exception types** when calling external systems (databases, HTTP APIs, file I/O) because these are common failure points that need distinct handling.

Apply **exception wrapping with cause** when translating between architectural layers — for example, catching `SQLException` in the repository layer and throwing a domain-specific `DataAccessException`.

Use **explicit logging** at application boundaries like REST controllers or message listeners, where exceptions transition from internal code to external responses. The practices matter most in code that runs in **production under load**, where debugging requires analyzing logs rather than stepping through a debugger.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Empty catch or invented default:** hides a failure and lets code continue without a defined result.
- **Blanket `catch (Throwable)`:** also catches Error values ordinary application code is usually unable to handle.
- **Dropping the cause during translation:** `new CustomException(message)` loses the link to the original failure; use the cause constructor when wrapping.
- **Logging at every layer:** creates repeated events for one incident.
- **Catching without an action:** let the exception reach a boundary that can recover, translate, or report it.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Catch with a purpose**: recover, translate, add context, or handle at a boundary.
- **Never silently swallow** an exception.
- **Preserve the cause** when wrapping.
- **Use specific types** and try-with-resources for cleanup.
- **Log once in the right place**, not automatically before every rethrow.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
My rule is to catch an exception only where I can make a useful decision. That may be recovering with a fallback, translating an infrastructure exception into a domain exception, adding meaningful context while preserving the cause, or mapping the failure at an application boundary. If I cannot improve the handling, I let it propagate.

I avoid empty catches, broad `catch (Throwable)`, and `return` from `finally`. I use try-with-resources for cleanup. I also do not log at every layer: logging and rethrowing usually duplicates one failure several times. The boundary that finally handles the error should normally log it once with the exception object so the stack trace and request context are preserved.

beats.text: Exception best practices are the habits that keep code debuggable in production. They're less about adding try-catch and more about what you do inside the catch. The capstone is centralized handling, where `@ControllerAdvice` catches exceptions across controllers in one spot.

Bad handling creates invisible failures. An empty catch makes a service look healthy while it quietly drops errors. A wrapped exception with no cause turns a five-minute fix into an hours-long hunt through the logs.

items: Never swallow. At minimum, log the error with the exception object.
Catch specific types. `IOException` beats a blind `catch (Exception)`.
Always pass the cause. Use `new ServiceException(msg, e)`, not just the message.
Log once at the boundary, not in every layer.
Use try-with-resources for anything AutoCloseable.

beats.text: Picture a Java 17 service that throws `IllegalArgumentException` on bad input. A single `@ControllerAdvice` maps it to a clean 400 and logs it once. Here's the non-obvious part. If a deeper catch had swallowed that error, the advice never fires, and the caller gets a silent success with no data.

items: Empty catch blocks. They hide failures and corrupt state silently.
`log.error(e.getMessage())`. It drops the stack trace you need most.
Catching `Throwable`. It swallows JVM errors that should crash the app.

speakable_v2.cap: Never swallow, log with the exception object, and always chain the cause. Those three habits prevent most production debugging nightmares.

questions.question: What is the correct way to log exceptions in Java?
questions.title: Correct Way to Log Exceptions in Java
questions.direct_answer: When a failure should be logged, pass the exception object to the logging API, for example `log.error("Could not load order {}", orderId, e)`, so the stack trace is retained. Choose the level from operational meaning, and avoid logging here if the same exception will be handled and logged at a higher boundary.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical logging knowledge — how to write debuggable code that helps troubleshoot production issues
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using log.error(e.getMessage()) which loses the stack trace in production logs, making debugging impossible
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention log levels (error vs warn vs info) and when to use each, plus the SLF4J parameterized logging syntax for performance

sections.title: Log the Exception Object, Not Just Its Message
sections.content:
Log an exception only when this layer owns a useful handling or observation decision. With SLF4J-style APIs, pass the exception object in the throwable position, commonly as the final argument: `log.error("Could not load order {}", orderId, e)`. Logging only `e.getMessage()` loses the exception type, stack, causes, and suppressed failures.

Use parameter placeholders instead of eager string concatenation. Choose `error`, `warn`, or another level from the service's operational policy, not simply from the Java class of the exception. A rejected user request is not automatically an error log, and a transient dependency issue may need rate-limited reporting or metrics.

Include useful identifiers such as a request or correlation ID, but do not log passwords, tokens, full payment data, or raw personal information. If a higher boundary will log the same failure with enough context, preserve and propagate it here rather than creating a duplicate event.

sections.title: Where the Stack Trace Goes
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A[Exception caught] --> B{How do you log it?} B -- log.error msg, e --> C[Full stack trace in logs] B -- log.error e.getMessage --> D[Only the text
stack trace lost] C --> E[Jump straight to the failing line] D --> F[Guess which class and line failed] style C fill:#bbf7d0 style D fill:#fecaca ```

sections.title: Correct Way to Log Exceptions in Java at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Right way|~pass the exception|log.error(msg, e)|framework adds the stack trace|e is the LAST arg
blue|Wrong way|~message only|log.error(e.getMessage())|stack trace is lost|cannot locate the failure
emerald|Levels|~match severity|error for bugs / infra|warn for expected-notable|info for state changes
rose|SLF4J tip|~parameterized|"order {}", id, e|lazy string building|avoid concatenation

sections.title: Wrong: only the message, stack trace gone
Right: exception as last argument, parameterized message
When to Use Each Log Level
sections.content:
Use **log.error** for unexpected failures that indicate bugs or infrastructure problems: database connection failures, `NullPointerException`, unhandled business logic errors, or external API timeouts. These require investigation and fixing.

Use **log.warn** for expected-but-notable conditions: invalid user input that fails validation, business rule violations like "insufficient inventory", or deprecated API usage. These are normal operations but worth tracking.

Use **log.info** for significant business events: user login, order created, payment completed.

Use **log.debug** during development for detailed flow tracing, but these shouldn't run in production due to volume. The exception-as-parameter pattern applies mainly to **error and warn levels** — if you're logging at info or debug, you typically don't have an exception object because those levels track normal flow, not failures.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Logging Only getMessage**: Using `log.error(e.getMessage())` or `log.error("Error: " + e.getMessage())` — this loses the stack trace completely, showing only the error text without any location information. When you see "Connection timeout" in production logs without knowing which service or method timed out, debugging becomes guesswork.
- **String Concatenation in Logs**: Writing `log.error("Failed for user " + userId, e)` — this builds the string even if error logging is disabled, wasting CPU. Use parameterized logging: `log.error("Failed for user {}", userId, e)` — the framework only formats the string if error level is enabled.
- **Wrong Parameter Order**: Putting the exception first like `log.error(e, "message")` — SLF4J expects the exception as the last parameter after message and placeholders, otherwise it might get interpreted as a placeholder value instead of being formatted with stack trace.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Keep the Throwable:** pass `e`, not only `e.getMessage()`.
- **Parameterized message:** use `{}` placeholders with the logger's supported overload.
- **Choose level by operations:** not every exception is an error event.
- **Safe context:** include correlation and domain IDs, never secrets or unnecessary personal data.
- **Avoid duplicates:** normally log at the boundary that owns final handling.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
When a failure should be logged, I pass the exception object to the logging API so the type, stack trace, causes, and suppressed exceptions are preserved. With SLF4J I might write `log.error("Could not load order {}", orderId, e)`, using a placeholder rather than string concatenation.

I choose the level from operational meaning, include safe correlation context, and avoid secrets or raw sensitive data. I also check ownership: if this method only rethrows and a higher boundary will log the same failure, I do not create a duplicate entry here.

questions.question: Why should exceptions not be used for ordinary control flow?
questions.title: Exceptions for Control Flow Anti-Pattern
questions.direct_answer: Do not use exceptions for an ordinary, frequent branch when the API can represent that outcome directly. Throwing normally captures diagnostic state and unwinds the stack, and it also hides the expected control flow. Exceptions are still correct for failures defined by an API; the issue is using them as a substitute for a normal condition, not an absolute ban.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of exception performance cost and semantic intent — does the candidate know when exceptions are appropriate
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using catch(NoSuchElementException) to check if a collection is empty — treating exceptions as if-statements
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain stack trace capture cost with numbers and give a concrete better alternative using Optional or if-checks

sections.title: Exceptions Are for the Exceptional
sections.content:
Exceptions are useful for reporting a failure from code that cannot complete its contract. They become a poor control-flow tool when an outcome is **ordinary and expected** and the API can represent it directly—for example, using `isEmpty()` instead of catching `NoSuchElementException` to detect an empty collection.

The main problem is clarity: a catch block looks like failure handling, so using it for a routine branch hides the normal path. Constructing and throwing an exception also commonly captures diagnostic state and unwinds the stack, which is usually more work than a direct branch. Exact speed ratios depend on the JVM, stack, and code, so fixed claims such as '1000 times slower' are not reliable guidance.

Do not turn this into an absolute ban. A parser, validator, or framework may define invalid input as an exception in its public contract. The caller should use the API as designed rather than duplicate work only to avoid every throw.

sections.title: Is This Really Exceptional?
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[A condition you must check] --> B{Happens on a normal path?}
    B -- Yes, often --> C[Use Optional, boolean, or if-check]
    B -- No, rare failure --> D[Throw an exception]
    C --> E[Cheap and clear intent]
    D --> F[Cost is justified, it's rare]
    style C fill:#bbf7d0
    style D fill:#fde68a
```

sections.title: Exceptions for Control Flow Anti-Pattern at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Anti-pattern|~exceptions as if/else|catch to branch|semantically wrong|"exception" means unexpected
blue|Why costly|~stack capture|new Exception() walks the stack|100-1000x slower|costly even if never logged
emerald|Use instead|~normal control flow|Optional for absence|if-check or boolean|return codes
rose|Rule|~rare vs frequent|>1 in 1000 is not exceptional|use plain logic|reserve for real failures

sections.title: Wrong: an exception as a not-found check
Right: Optional and explicit checks express intent
When to Use Exceptions vs Alternatives
sections.content:
Use exceptions for **truly unexpected failures**: `IOException` when the disk is full, `SQLException` when the database connection drops, or `IllegalStateException` when your object is in an invalid state due to a programming bug.

Use **if-checks** for expected conditions you validate regularly: checking if input is null, if a list is empty, or if a number is in a valid range — these happen on normal code paths thousands of times.

Use **Optional** when a value might legitimately not exist and that's a normal outcome: `findById` might not find a record, `parseDate` might encounter invalid format.

Use **boolean returns** for yes/no decisions where both outcomes are equally valid: `isValid`, `exists`, `canProcess`. The rule of thumb: if the condition happens more than once per thousand executions, it's not exceptional — use normal control flow.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Exception as Null Check**: Using try-catch `NullPointerException` instead of `if (obj != null)` — this is thousands of times slower and completely unclear to readers what you're checking. Every NPE costs microseconds in stack trace creation for what should be a nanosecond comparison.
- **Exception for Empty Check**: Using `catch (NoSuchElementException)` or `catch (IndexOutOfBoundsException)` to detect empty collections — just call `isEmpty` or use `Optional` instead.
- **Exception for Validation**: Throwing `NumberFormatException` to check if a string is numeric, then catching it — use a regex or try-parse pattern with `Optional` instead. This creates unnecessary exception objects on every invalid input, which in a web form validation scenario means exceptions on every user typo.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Use exceptions for failures** defined by an API or operation contract.
- **Avoid them for routine branches** that have a direct query or result type.
- **Why:** hidden normal flow plus stack capture and unwinding work.
- **No fixed ratio:** cost depends on JVM and call stack.
- **Follow the API:** do not pre-check in a racy or duplicated way merely to avoid an exception.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I avoid exceptions as a substitute for an ordinary branch. For example, I check `isEmpty()` rather than calling `getFirst()` and catching `NoSuchElementException` as the normal empty result. The direct form is clearer, and throwing an exception usually captures diagnostic state and unwinds the stack.

I would not state a universal speed multiplier or ban exceptions from every expected failure. Some APIs deliberately report invalid input or a failed operation with an exception. The important distinction is whether I am following a failure contract or using throw and catch as a disguised `if` statement.

questions.question: Why should you not log and rethrow the same exception?
questions.title: Log-and-Rethrow Anti-Pattern in Java
questions.direct_answer: Logging and rethrowing the same failure at several layers creates duplicate log events for one incident. Usually a lower layer should add context by wrapping with the original cause and let the final handling boundary log once. Logging before rethrowing can be justified when that layer owns unique diagnostic information, but it should be a deliberate exception, not the default.

interviewer_intent.testing: Production-quality exception handling awareness — understanding how exceptions propagate in layered architectures
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Logging in every catch block and then rethrowing — three layers means three log entries for the same error
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the correct pattern: log once at the top (global handler or boundary), let exceptions propagate without logging in intermediate layers

sections.title: Log the Error Once, Not at Every Layer
sections.content:
Logging and then rethrowing at every application layer often produces several records for one failure. A repository, service, controller, and global handler can otherwise emit the same stack trace four times, which distorts counts and alerts.

The usual design is to preserve or translate the exception below and log once where propagation ends: an HTTP exception handler, message listener, scheduled-job runner, or process boundary. Translation should retain the cause and add only context meaningful to the new abstraction.

This is not an absolute prohibition. A lower layer may own unique diagnostic data that will not travel with the exception, or an audit policy may require a separate event. In that case, log deliberately, avoid sensitive values, and distinguish the event from the final failure log.

sections.title: One Error, One Log Entry
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Repository throws SQLException] --> B[Service: rethrow, do not log]
    B --> C[Controller layer]
    C --> D[ControllerAdvice logs once]
    D --> E[Return one clean error response]
    style D fill:#bbf7d0
    style E fill:#bbf7d0
```

sections.title: Log-and-Rethrow Anti-Pattern in Java at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Anti-pattern|~log then rethrow|each layer logs again|N duplicate stack traces|noisy logs
blue|Why bad|~hard to analyze|looks like N errors|alerts fire many times|wasted storage
emerald|Right way|~log once at the top|@RestControllerAdvice|intermediate layers propagate|wrap without logging
rose|Wrapping is ok|~translate the type|new ServiceException(msg, e)|adds context|just do not also log it

sections.title: Wrong: every layer logs the same error
Right: rethrow silently, log once at the boundary
When to Log vs When to Rethrow
sections.content:
**Log once at the application boundary**: in your `@RestControllerAdvice` global exception handler, in message listener error handlers, or in scheduled job catch blocks — places where the exception stops propagating and gets converted to a response or retry decision. **Rethrow without logging in intermediate layers**: in service methods that catch and wrap exceptions to add context (like wrapping `SQLException` in `DataAccessException`), and in repository methods that translate persistence exceptions to domain exceptions. **Never log and rethrow** in the same catch block unless you're adding significant new context that wasn't in the original exception.

Use **logging without rethrowing** only at terminal points where the error is fully handled and won't propagate further, like in async callbacks or fire-and-forget operations.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Logging in Every Catch Block**: Writing `log.error` in every layer's catch block before rethrowing — a three-layer application logs the same `SQLException` three times, making it look like three separate errors occurred.
- **Using printStackTrace**: Calling `e.printStackTrace()` in catch blocks, which writes to `System.err` not your logging framework — this output doesn't get captured by log aggregation tools and isn't structured with timestamps or log levels.
- **Logging Then Swallowing**: Logging the exception but not rethrowing it when the calling code needs to know the operation failed — this creates silent failures where the error is logged but the application continues with bad state, causing confusing downstream errors. The service layer thinks the order was created but it actually failed, leading to inventory problems that manifest hours later.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Problem:** every layer logging one exception creates duplicates.
- **Normal rule:** propagate or translate below; log where handling ends.
- **Preserve cause:** wrapping is not a reason to discard the original.
- **Boundaries:** HTTP handler, listener, job runner, or process entry point.
- **Exception:** unique diagnostics or audit requirements may justify a separate, clearly different event.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I normally avoid logging and rethrowing the same failure at every layer because one incident becomes several stack traces and distorts monitoring. Intermediate layers should let it propagate or translate it at a real abstraction boundary while preserving the cause. The HTTP handler, message listener, or job runner that finally handles the failure normally logs it once.

It is a guideline rather than a law. If a layer owns diagnostic information that cannot be carried safely with the exception, or must emit an audit event, it can log a distinct event deliberately. I avoid duplicate wording and sensitive data.

questions.question: Is it bad practice to catch NullPointerException instead of fixing the null?
questions.title: Catching NullPointerException vs Fixing the Root Cause
questions.direct_answer: Catching `NullPointerException` around a broad block is usually a code smell because it cannot tell an expected missing value from an unrelated null bug in that block. Define the null contract and handle absence before dereferencing, or validate required values. A narrow catch is reasonable only when a specific API explicitly uses NPE as part of a contract and the caller can handle that exact failure.

interviewer_intent.testing: Code quality mindset — does the candidate fix problems or mask them with exception handling
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Wrapping code in try-catch NullPointerException when the real fix is to not have null in the first place
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain Optional as the modern Java approach to nulls, and Objects.requireNonNull for fail-fast validation at method entry points

sections.title: An NPE Is a Bug, Not a Condition to Catch
sections.content:
A broad `catch (NullPointerException)` usually hides **which expression was unexpectedly null**. It may catch the null you anticipated, but it can also catch a different defect introduced later in the same block. That makes normal absence and programming errors indistinguishable.

Handle a known nullable value explicitly before using it. Validate a required input with `Objects.requireNonNull`, use a normal branch for a nullable field, or use `Optional` selectively when it makes a return contract clearer. Java itself has no universal non-null-by-default type system; annotations and project conventions can add that policy.

There are narrow exceptions to the guideline. If a documented API deliberately throws NPE for a particular invalid input and the caller must translate that exact result, a very small catch may be defensible. It should not surround unrelated work or silently continue.

sections.title: Catch the NPE or Fix the Null?
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A[Code hits a possible null] --> B{Catch the NPE?} B -- Catch it --> C[Bug hidden
other NPEs swallowed too] B -- Fix the source --> D{Is absence normal?} D -- Yes --> E[Use Optional] D -- No --> F[requireNonNull at entry] style C fill:#fecaca style E fill:#bbf7d0 style F fill:#bbf7d0 ```

sections.title: Catching NullPointerException vs Fixing the Root Cause at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Bad practice|~catch NPE|masks a real bug|the null is still there|swallows other NPEs too
blue|Why|~NPE is a programming error|missing init or validation|not an expected case|fix the source
emerald|Fix the null|~prevent it|Optional for absence|Objects.requireNonNull|null checks at entry
rose|Modern Java|~non-null by default|Optional return types|@NonNull / @Nullable|never return null collections

sections.title: Wrong: catch NPE and hide the missing user
Right: Optional for absence, requireNonNull for contracts
When to Use Optional vs Validation
sections.content:
Use **Optional** when a value might legitimately not exist and that's a normal business scenario: `findById` might not find a record, a user's middle name might be empty, or parsing a date from user input might fail. Optional makes the "might be absent" case explicit in your method signature, forcing callers to handle it.

Use **Objects.requireNonNull** at method entry points for parameters that should never be null — this implements **fail-fast validation** and throws immediately with a clear message.

Use **explicit null checks with if-statements** when you need to handle the null case with specific business logic, like `if (discount == null)` then use a default discount rate. Avoid broad **try-catch NullPointerException** — if you're tempted to catch NPE, your design has a problem. Either the caller should pass non-null values, or your method should return Optional to signal that absence is possible.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Catching NPE as Validation**: Wrapping code in try-catch `NullPointerException` to check if an object is null — this is wildly inefficient compared to `if (obj != null)` and semantically wrong because you're treating a bug as expected flow.
- **Returning Null from Methods**: Having methods return null to signal "not found" instead of returning `Optional` — this forces every caller to remember to null-check, leading to NPE bugs scattered throughout the codebase. The method signature doesn't communicate that absence is possible.
- **Defensive Null Checks Everywhere**: Adding `if (obj != null)` before every single object use because you don't trust your code — this indicates missing validation at entry points. Fix the root cause by ensuring nulls can't enter your system rather than checking everywhere.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Broad NPE catches hide the source** and may swallow an unrelated defect.
- **Handle known absence directly** before an operation dereferences it.
- **Validate required inputs** with a clear contract and message.
- **Use Optional selectively**, commonly for return values where absence is normal.
- **Non-null by default is a project policy**, not a universal Java type-system rule.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Catching NullPointerException around a large block is usually wrong because the catch cannot identify which expression was null and may hide a separate bug. I handle a known nullable value explicitly before dereferencing it, validate required arguments, and use Optional where it makes a return contract clearer.

Java does not make every ordinary reference non-null by default, so the project must express that through API design, annotations, and tests. I would catch NPE only in a very narrow adapter if a documented API deliberately uses that exception for the exact condition I am translating.

questions.question: What is fail-fast and how does it relate to exception handling?
questions.title: Fail-Fast Principle in Java Exception Handling
questions.direct_answer: Fail-fast means rejecting invalid input or state at the nearest trustworthy boundary, before later work hides the real cause. Use a clear precondition and a suitable exception such as `NullPointerException` from `requireNonNull`, `IllegalArgumentException`, or `IllegalStateException`. Validate once at the owning boundary; it does not mean repeating every check in every private method.

interviewer_intent.testing: Defensive programming awareness and practical exception use — does the candidate validate inputs proactively
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Letting bad input propagate deep into the code and cause confusing NPEs or logic errors far from the source
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how IllegalArgumentException and Objects.requireNonNull implement the fail-fast principle with concrete examples

sections.title: Fail-Fast Means Throw Early
sections.content:
**Fail-fast** means reporting an invalid input or state close to where the program can identify it clearly, before unrelated work turns it into a confusing later failure. A constructor can reject an invalid object state, an API boundary can validate a request, and startup can reject missing required configuration.

Use the exception that matches the contract. `Objects.requireNonNull` throws `NullPointerException` for a required reference, `IllegalArgumentException` fits an invalid argument value, and `IllegalStateException` fits an operation that is invalid for the object's current state. Messages should name the failed rule without exposing secrets.

'Early' means the nearest boundary that owns the invariant, not necessarily every method call. Repeating expensive checks at every private helper adds noise. External validation also does not replace database constraints or security checks; each protects a different boundary.

sections.title: Fail-Fast vs Fail-Slow
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A[Bad input arrives] --> B{Validate at entry?} B -- Yes, fail-fast --> C[Throw now
clear message at the source] B -- No, fail-slow --> D[Travels deep into the code] D --> E[Cryptic NPE far from the cause] style C fill:#bbf7d0 style E fill:#fecaca ```

sections.title: Fail-Fast Principle in Java Exception Handling at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Fail-fast|~detect early|validate at method entry|throw before processing|error near the root cause
blue|Tools|~entry checks|Objects.requireNonNull|IllegalArgumentException|IllegalStateException
emerald|Why|~a clear stack trace|error at the source|not five calls later|easy to map to input
rose|Where|~external boundaries|public APIs / controllers|constructors|startup config

sections.title: Wrong: bad input fails deep and cryptically
Right: validate at the entry, throw immediately
When to Apply Fail-Fast Validation
sections.content:
Apply fail-fast validation at **public API method entry points** in your service and controller layers — these are where external input enters your controlled domain. Validate method parameters that come from **user input, external APIs, or message queues** because these sources can't be trusted.

Use fail-fast for **constructor parameters** when creating domain objects — an `Order` with null items or negative quantity should never be instantiated.

Apply it to **configuration values** at application startup — if a required environment variable is missing, fail immediately rather than starting in a broken state.

Use it for **state preconditions** in stateful objects — if `processPayment` is called before `validateCart`, throw `IllegalStateException`. Don't overdo fail-fast validation in **private helper methods** called from already-validated public methods — that's redundant.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Skipping Validation on Nulls**: Assuming parameters will never be null because "the caller should know better" — this violates fail-fast because you let null propagate until it causes an NPE somewhere deep in the logic.
- **Validation in the Wrong Layer**: Putting validation logic in the repository or database layer instead of the service entry point — this lets bad data travel through your business logic before failing with a database constraint error that's harder to map back to the invalid input.
- **Generic Error Messages**: Throwing exceptions with messages like "Invalid input" or "Bad request" that don't specify which parameter or constraint failed — this defeats the point of fail-fast. Use specific messages like "customerId cannot be null" or "discount must be between 0 and 100".

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Fail-fast:** report a violated rule near the boundary that owns it.
- **Required reference:** `Objects.requireNonNull`.
- **Bad argument:** `IllegalArgumentException`; **bad object state:** `IllegalStateException`.
- **Clear message:** name the rule without leaking sensitive data.
- **No ritual duplication:** validate at meaningful trust and invariant boundaries.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Fail-fast means rejecting invalid input or state where the program can still explain the real rule that was broken, instead of allowing a later unrelated failure. I validate constructor invariants, public request boundaries, and required startup configuration with an exception that fits the contract.

`requireNonNull` handles a required reference, IllegalArgumentException fits a bad value, and IllegalStateException fits an operation invalid in the current state. I validate at the boundary that owns the rule rather than copying every check into every private helper, and I still keep database and security constraints where those boundaries need them.

speakable_v2.hook: Fail-fast means you throw the moment bad data enters a method. Not three layers later, when a cryptic NPE pops up far from the real cause.

beats.text: Fail-fast is a defensive habit. You validate inputs at the start of a method and throw right away when they're wrong. The error lands at the entry point, and `@ExceptionHandler` maps an exception to a response cleanly above it.

Without fail-fast, a null id slips into `findById` and blows up 20 lines later inside a query builder. The stack trace points at the builder, not the bad call. Now you're tracing backward to find where the null started.

items: `Objects.requireNonNull(param, msg)` throws a clear NPE on null.
`IllegalArgumentException` covers bad values, like negative ids.
`IllegalStateException` covers a wrong-order call.
Validate at the entry, before any business logic runs.

beats.text: Picture a Java 17 endpoint that throws `IllegalArgumentException` the instant an id is negative. A single `@ControllerAdvice` maps it to a 400. Here's the non-obvious part. `requireNonNull` throws an NPE, not an IAE, even though null is arguably an illegal argument. That's a Java convention worth knowing.

items: Validating in the middle of a method. Check at entry, before side effects.
Using `IllegalArgumentException` for null. Reach for `requireNonNull` instead.
